analysis.one_liner: Would turn a presidential commission's Social Security overhaul, including personal retirement accounts, into federal law.
analysis.headline: Four House Democrats introduced the bill on March 20, 2002; it was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and died without a hearing or vote when the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have enacted, word-for-word by reference, "Reform Model 3" from President Bush's Commission to Strengthen Social Security — a plan whose models redirect part of Social Security payroll taxes into individually owned investment accounts while slowing the growth of guaranteed benefits. It was introduced by Rep. Robert Matsui along with three of the top House Democrats: Minority Leader Richard Gephardt, Whip Nancy Pelosi, and Ways and Means Democrat Charles Rangel. The committee it went to never took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, financial firms would have gained a vast new business managing individual retirement accounts carved out of Social Security payroll taxes. Workers would have owned accounts they could invest, but the guaranteed, inflation-protected benefit that Social Security pays today would have been reduced, and the transition would have required substantial new government borrowing.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Financial firms managing new retirement accounts

how_it_helps.text: The bill writes into law "Reform Model 3" from the President's Commission to Strengthen Social Security, a December 2001 report titled "Strengthening Social Security and Creating Personal Wealth for All Americans."

Under the commission's model approach, a portion of each worker's Social Security payroll contribution would go into an individually owned account invested in stocks and bonds, which the bill's own subject list reflects through entries for savings accounts and payroll deductions.
The bill directs the Social Security Commissioner and Treasury Secretary to write any regulations needed to operate the new system, effective 180 days after enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Workers would bear investment risk in place of part of their guaranteed benefit, and taxpayers would cover the cost of funding both the new accounts and existing benefits during the transition. Retirees and people nearing retirement would face the most uncertainty about what they would actually receive.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers and taxpayers, through added risk and debt

drawbacks.text: The bill does not contain the plan itself; it adopts a commission report by reference and overrides the Social Security Act and the tax code "to the extent necessary," so Congress would be voting on a plan whose statutory details it never wrote down.

The commission's models would reduce guaranteed benefits relative to current law and shift retirement income risk from a government guarantee onto individual investment accounts, so workers retiring in a market downturn would have less protection than under the current program.

Redirecting payroll contributions into private accounts creates a transition funding gap: contributions going into accounts are no longer available to pay current retirees, requiring new borrowing or deeper benefit cuts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The trade is stark: individual accounts offer the chance of higher market returns and inheritable wealth, but they replace a guaranteed benefit with one that depends on investment results, and the transition would be expensive. Whether that trade helps any given worker depends entirely on how the markets perform during their retirement — the current program's main feature, predictability, is what the change would take away.

outcome.mechanism: The Ways and Means Committee never scheduled a hearing or vote, so the bill simply expired when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Matsui introduced the bill on March 20, 2002, joined by Reps. Gephardt, Pelosi, and Rangel as original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day it was introduced.
Three Democratic members cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.
The action history shows no further steps after the referral — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the Congress ended.
The bill's entire operative text is a single sentence enacting the commission's Reform Model 3 into law, superseding existing Social Security and tax provisions as needed.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Social Security's current guaranteed structure stayed untouched, and members of both parties never had to take a recorded vote on an overhaul of the nation's largest retirement program. The bill's death also kept financial firms from gaining the account-management business it would have created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Social Security kept its current structure

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred; all four sponsors and all three cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican ever acted on the bill.

industries.note: Had it passed, the bill would have made investment firms the permanent administrators of a large slice of Social Security contributions, giving them a built-in stream of fees from a public program. Workers' money would flow through these firms regardless of market results, while the guaranteed benefit shrank.

industries.industry: Current Social Security beneficiaries and workers paying payroll taxes
industries.note: The bill would have reduced the growth of guaranteed benefits while giving workers individual accounts, so the same group would have gained one thing and lost another. Its failure preserved the current guarantee.
